note: Pond Advent, 1-24 Dec 2026. One email a day, sent by .github/workflows/send-advent.yml (automation/newsletter/send-advent.mjs) to the Pond Advent list. Each day: subject, paragraphs (HTML allowed, keep links ?ref=advent), and one button. Written in Sam's voice: I, not we.

days.subject: Door 1: a Christmas Day you can see coming
p: Hello, it's Sam. Door one, and it's the one I'd want first: a free Christmas visual timetable.

Christmas Day throws the usual routine out of the window. Seeing the day in pictures, in order, takes a lot of the worry out of it. There are 20 picture cards (presents, visitors, car journey, quiet time, bed), a first/then board and an "I need a break" card.
Tip: go through it the day before, and again in the morning. If plans change, change the cards. A surprise on paper is easier than a surprise out loud.

days.subject: Door 2: something to send the grandparents
p: If you're going to spend Christmas explaining your child (or yourself) to the relatives, let a page do it.
The free autism guide is two pages of plain English, written for the people around an autistic person, not the person themselves. No clinical words, nothing that makes anyone feel got at.
Tip: send it a week before the visit, not on the doorstep. People take things in better when they can read on their own.

days.subject: Door 3: the quiet room
p: Today's door is a small one that makes a big difference: a quiet room.

Pick it before the day. Somewhere with a door, low light, nothing expected. Anyone can go there without being followed or asked why. Ear defenders, a tablet or a favourite thing are tools, not bad manners.
I wrote up the rest of what helps (presents, food, visits, the days after) here.

days.subject: Door 4: ADHD, explained properly
p: ADHD is one of the worst-named conditions going. It isn't a shortage of attention: it's attention that won't take instructions about where to point.
The free ADHD guide explains that in plain English, for the partner, the parent or the boss who thinks you just need to try harder.

days.subject: Door 5: a card that says it for you
p: When it all gets too much, explaining what you need is the first thing to go. So make the card now, while it's easy.

The free "how to help me" card maker takes a minute: what happens when it gets too much, what helps, what doesn't. It prints credit-card size for a wallet or the back of a phone case. Nothing you type is sent or saved.
Make one for a child to keep in their coat pocket, too.

days.subject: Door 6: why the fairy lights are a lot
p: Most people know about five senses. There are eight, and in December all of them are turned up: lights, music, crowds, scratchy jumpers, new smells, new food.
The free sensory guide explains sensory differences for the people who keep saying "it's only a bit of noise".

days.subject: Door 7: what to do when it's too much
p: A practical one today. When sensory overload hits, the first thing that helps is less: less noise, less light, fewer words, fewer people.
I wrote down what helps in the moment and afterwards, for you or for someone you're with.

days.subject: Door 8: PDA, for the people who say "just make them"
p: PDA describes a profile where everyday demands feel threatening, including demands the person actually wants to meet. Christmas is wall-to-wall demands, even the nice ones.
The free PDA guide is for the relatives who think it's spoiling. It isn't.

days.subject: Door 9: presents without the pressure
p: A tip for the presents. Opening them in front of everyone, with everyone watching your face, is a lot.
Try: a few at a time across the day, or in private. Wrap in clear paper or don't wrap at all, so there are no surprises. Agree beforehand that no one has to perform delight.
And if a present is wrong, "thank you, I'll have a proper look later" is a whole answer.

days.subject: Door 10: autistic and ADHD at once
p: Being both autistic and ADHD isn't the two lists added together. It's two nervous systems asking for opposite things at the same time: routine and novelty, quiet and stimulation.
The free AuDHD guide explains it for the people who find you a contradiction.

days.subject: Door 11: what to say to the grandparents
p: Day two was the guide. Today is the conversation: what to tell grandparents before Christmas, what to ask them to do, and what to ask them not to do.
Short, practical, and written by someone who's had the conversation.

days.subject: Door 12: one page, built for your brain
p: Halfway. Today's door is a planner page made for you.

Answer three questions (how you like a day laid out, how you track your energy, what you keep forgetting) and you get a free daily page built around the answers, with your name on it. Print as many as you like.

days.subject: Door 13: anxiety at Christmas
p: Anxiety is often the result of being neurodivergent in a world that isn't built for you, rather than a separate thing. December doesn't help.
The free anxiety guide explains it gently, for the people who say "just don't worry about it".

days.subject: Door 14: when the tank is empty
p: If you're more tired than tired, losing words, and the things you usually manage have stopped being manageable, it might be burnout rather than a bad week.
I wrote about what autistic burnout is, what it looks like, and what helps. The short answer: less, for longer than feels reasonable.

days.subject: Door 15: more than clumsy
p: Dyspraxia gets reduced to clumsiness, which misses most of it. It affects planning and sequencing: of movement, and often of everything else too. Think wrapping paper, Sellotape and a list of who's bringing what.
The free dyspraxia guide explains it in plain English.

days.subject: Door 16: feelings without names
p: Alexithymia isn't the absence of feelings. It's having them at full strength with no reliable way to name them. "Are you having a nice time?" can be a genuinely hard question.
The free guide explains it for the people who keep asking.

days.subject: Door 17: "you're just lazy"
p: If someone in the family thinks ADHD is an excuse, this one's for you: how to explain ADHD to family, what to ask for, and what you don't owe them.
Christmas is a lot of time together. It's worth having the words ready.
button: How to explain ADHD to family

days.subject: Door 18: when the words won't come
p: Some people can talk easily at home and not at all at Aunty's house. That's situational mutism (often still called selective mutism, though nothing about it is selected).
The free guide explains it, and why "come on, say hello" makes it worse.

days.subject: Door 19: dyslexia and the Christmas card list
p: Dyslexia has almost nothing to do with intelligence, and a lot to do with how the brain handles the sounds inside words. Cards, labels and quizzes can be quietly exhausting.
The free dyslexia guide explains it for everyone else.

days.subject: Door 20: when family won't accept it
p: Late diagnosis, and the family brushes it off, makes jokes, or tells you to keep it quiet. It hurts, and it's common.
I wrote about why it happens, what you don't owe them, and what you could hand them instead of explaining your whole life again.
button: When family won't accept a diagnosis

days.subject: Door 21: the longest night
p: Today's the winter solstice, the longest night of the year. If December feels heavy, you're not imagining it.
Depression among neurodivergent people is very often the accumulated cost of years of masking and unmet needs. The free guide is gentle about it. And from tomorrow, the days get longer.

days.subject: Door 22: the crunching, the chewing, the crackers
p: If certain small sounds (chewing, crunching, cutlery on plates) bring instant rage or panic, you're not being difficult. That's misophonia, and Christmas dinner is its final boss.
The free guide explains it. Tip: background music at the table helps more than you'd think.

days.subject: Door 23: which cousin is this?
p: If you've ever walked past someone you know and quietly built a life around covering for it, there's a name for that: face blindness.
The free guide explains it. Tip for the big day: "remind me who's who?" is fine, and name stickers are hilarious and useful.

days.subject: Door 24: from me, from the pond
p: Last door. Thank you for opening them with me.
Behind this one is everything: all 23 free Pond Guides, to print or forward to whoever needs them this Christmas. And the visual timetable again, in case tomorrow needs it.
Whatever tomorrow looks like for you (big, small, loud, quiet, or under a blanket) I hope it's kind. Sam 🐸
